query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) outside Nb-Ta and Ti-rich matrices, the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) is primarily governed by the average electron count per atom (valence electron concentration, VEC) and the degree of chemical disorder, which together modulate the density of states at the Fermi level and electron-phonon coupling strength. Specifically, HEAs with VEC near optimal values for known superconductors and moderate disorder (retaining a single-phase solid solution) will exhibit higher Tc, while excessive disorder or deviation from optimal VEC will suppress superconductivity.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy solid solution containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent, not dominated by Nb-Ta or Ti-rich matrices.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the alloy composition to adjust the average VEC and degree of chemical disorder, while maintaining a single-phase solid solution.
generation.conditions: Ambient pressure, low temperature (below 10 K), and absence of magnetic impurities; all samples must be single-phase solid solutions.
generation.structural_mediator: Average electron count per atom (VEC) and chemical disorder (quantified by configurational entropy and local atomic environment).
generation.mechanism: The VEC determines the density of states at the Fermi level, influencing electron-phonon coupling and thus Tc. Chemical disorder affects scattering and can either enhance or suppress superconductivity depending on its impact on electron mobility and phonon modes.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs with VEC near optimal values for conventional superconductors (e.g., VEC ≈ 5–7) and moderate disorder will show measurable superconducting transitions with Tc comparable to or slightly lower than those of ordered alloys with similar VEC. Alloys with excessive disorder or VEC far from optimal will show suppressed or absent superconductivity.
generation.baseline: A single-phase HEA with VEC outside the optimal range and/or excessive disorder, expected to show no superconducting transition above 2 K.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis applies only to single-phase solid solutions with at least five elements at ≥5 at.% each, not dominated by Nb-Ta or Ti-rich matrices, and without strong magnetic impurities.
generation.uncertainty: Lack of direct experimental evidence for superconductivity in HEAs outside Nb-Ta and Ti-rich systems; uncertainty in the precise optimal VEC range and the quantitative effect of disorder.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEAs with systematically varied VEC and controlled disorder, all as single-phase solid solutions. Measure Tc via resistivity and magnetic susceptibility down to 2 K.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HEAs with VEC near optimal values and moderate disorder consistently fail to exhibit superconductivity above 2 K, or if Tc does not correlate with VEC and disorder as predicted, the hypothesis is falsified.
